blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-skeptic-1 (The plan assumes one e-mail is one person, which its own context contradicts) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-skeptic-2 (Merged records are deleted with no way back) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
Since an e-mail address identifies exactly one person, the job groups
customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The design's own Context says the opposite: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." Under the decision as written, the nightly job merges those distinct buyers into the oldest one, moves every buyer's orders to that one person and deletes the others' records along with their names and billing addresses — the wrong thing built, and data lost. Drop the assumption or ground it: choose a matching key that separates shared mailboxes (e.g. e-mail plus name and billing address, or only records created by guest checkout with identical details), or exclude known shared mailboxes. Then add a spec scenario "Shared mailbox, different buyers" whose THEN is that both records remain, and cover it in task 1.1.
findings.title: The plan assumes one e-mail is one person, which its own context contradicts

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The deletion is a one-way door: the deleted records' `name` and `billing_address` (app/schema.sql, NOT NULL columns) are gone, and a wrong merge cannot be undone because nothing records which orders belonged to which customer. Add a way back before deleting — a merge log of the moved order ids and the removed rows, or a soft delete / `merged_into` column — and a staged rollout (a dry-run mode reporting the groups it would merge before the first real run). Add the corresponding requirement and task.
findings.title: Merged records are deleted with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The only scenarios are "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate". The design matches on "lower-cased e-mail", but no scenario says that `Ada@Example.org` and `ada@example.org` are merged, so the case rule is not verifiable. Missing too: a group of three or more records, two records with the same `created_at` (which one is "the oldest"), and a guest checkout that inserts a customer or an order while the job runs. Add a scenario for each case the job must handle, and list them in task 1.1.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path

findings.recommendation: The What Changes adds "A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address." — something that must be scheduled, monitored and stopped if it misbehaves — yet the operations box is unticked with no reason, so no expert reviews how it runs. Tick it, or keep it unticked with the reason on its line.
findings.title: Operations is unticked although the plan adds a scheduled job
